event: VXE 628 fuselage flown with VXE 501 wing and other parts lost its center wing systems during transition to VTOL for landing; the land abort failed and the aircraft crashed and was destroyed.
component: XCOMM / center wing interface (CW Ethernet, payload 12 V bus, VTOL AP and ADP links)
failure_mode: Simultaneous loss of payload and CW Ethernet, payload 12 V drop and CAN timeouts to VTOL AP and air data at VTOL transition, consistent with a large transient or short on the XCOMM rather than a simple CW disconnect
contributing: Flight firmware about two years out of date and mismatched (AP 6.05m, XComm 4.60, VTOL 1.44)
Airspeed faults left the fixed wing land abort without air data
Payload retract command at landing coincided with the fault
Aircraft assembled from two tails (628 fuselage, 501 components)

evidence.quote: VTOL data stops updating on XComm logs about the same time as CAN timeouts are recorded for both VTOL and Air data.
It seems like whatever fault occured, it affected multiple measurements and busses on the XCOM
2789.879 – Payload Voltage fault recorded (Voltage drops below 12V)
@Cameron Chapman I believe all software investigations have been complete. CW failure cause unknown.
Investigation updated. CW stopped functioning during VTOL transition resulting in a failed land abort.

team_root_cause: Aside from using flight firmware multiple iterations and flight-safety warnings out of date, the avionics lost communication with the CW during VTOL transition resulting in a failed land abort. Land abort likely failed due to no airspeed data, and there is log data to indicate airspeed faults after the landing abort started.

would_settle_it.what: Zoomed timeline of payload voltage, retract current and Ethernet drops to see which signal failed first
Bench test and inspect XCOMM (as in VIT2-252, C20 / regulator damage) and CW harness for short or burn evidence
Vehicle Investigation VXEP-732.pptx with voltage and bus timeline
XComm voltages, ground isolation FET state and VTOL throttles at 2786 to 2790 s

reasoning: Logs show a land abort at VTOL transition, then payload and CW Ethernet drops, a payload voltage fault below 12 V and CAN timeouts to the VTOL AP and air data within a few hundred milliseconds. Engineers agree this looks like a transient or short on the XCOMM side rather than a CW unplug, but no hardware was inspected and the investigator closed with the CW failure cause unknown. So the evidence narrows it to the XCOMM / CW power and data interface, not one part.
notes: Aircraft was the 628 fuselage reconfigured as tail 501 with 501 wing and components, so tail given as 628+501. Investigation was first halted for outdated firmware and later reopened. ENG-2992 (VXE 444, XCOMM retract spike and AP C20 failure) read only as a comparison case; its raw log attachments belong to a different aircraft and were not read. FS2-2321 AD PDFs and spreadsheet not read (firmware list taken from the report slides). RMA-359 induction PDF has no text (scanned).

event: VXE 510, no payload at forward CG, pitched up sharply (over 36 degrees) and then down right after the forward transition during LM testing; the flight continued normally.
failure_mode: Large pitch up overshoot as VTOL motors shut down at end of transition while rear motors were still holding nose-up trim
contributing: Forward CG no-payload configuration
Rear lift motors (LR and RR) still carrying significant trim at motor cutoff
Same overshoot seen on a second flight (T95_V510_241023_132040)

evidence.quote: It looks like toward the end of transition the vtol motors were holding a good bit of trim (LR/RR motors still on significantly, RR > 0.6).
no payload would put the aircraft at forward limit for the flight.
There were two flights that had the large overshoot - T95_V510_241022_085416_pack and T95_V510_241023_132040_pack.
The configs and software versions looked correct to me.

team_root_cause: It is unclear what caused the pitch up but subsequent flights looked normal so the issue is likely due to environmental factors.

would_settle_it.what: Elevator command and trim, pitch rate and rear motor throttles at motor cutoff compared with other forward CG first flights
Elevator zero, range and backlash, and measured CG location

reasoning: The data show rear motors still holding nose-up trim at the end of transition and the pitch-up starting as they powered down, with the aircraft at its forward CG limit. Software and configs looked correct, no physical inspection was done, and the overshoot repeated on a second flight, which argues against a one-off environmental cause. Evidence does not get past the symptom.
notes: Team Root Cause states the cause is unclear and offers likely environmental factors as a best estimate (closed Bermuda Triangle), so scored as no team answer. Motors are named only as LR/RR in the text describing trim, not as a failure position.

event: Edge FLOPS flights on VXE 674 and 734 with new main batteries 2101 and 2088 showed a GCS state of charge about 20 percent higher than the COTS battery checker after landing (62 percent vs 37 percent).
failure_mode: Checker computes SoC from a generic Li-ion discharge curve that does not match the Amicell main battery chemistry, so it under-reads
contributing: No guidance in manuals to ignore checker SoC for Amicell packs

evidence.quote: For example, my flight specifically was reading 62% before recovery and read 37% on the battery checker post flight.
The cell chemistry of our Amicell batteries are not the same as those used in Li-ion batteries.
It was determined that the Batter Checker in the FSK provided incorrect SoC data based on an incorrect battery model in the checker for the Amicell battery chemistry.
Integration of the power consumption predicts about a 45% SOC on landing

team_root_cause:
The issue comes down to the use of COTS battery checkers and the Li-ion model included in the battery checkers to assess the state of charge of our Amicell battery. The cell chemistry of our Amicell batteries have a different SoC discharge curve compared to that of which the cell checkers are programmed to.
[embedded: image-20241030-204746.png]
Li-ion discharge curve
[embedded: image-20241030-212419.png]
Measured Amicell discharge curve

would_settle_it.what: Measured Amicell discharge curve versus the checker's Li-ion curve at the reported pack voltages
Logged pack voltage and integrated energy at landing to confirm the aircraft SoC was right

reasoning: Engineers traced the gap to the COTS checker, whose SoC model assumes a Li-ion curve that does not fit the Amicell cells, and showed the measured Amicell curve. In the related VXEP-720 case the aircraft's own estimate matched energy integration, so the aircraft reading was not shown to be wrong. The reported aircraft fault is unfounded; the discrepancy comes from the ground checker.
notes: Ticket canceled; corrective action tracked in VXEP-720. The description first said the checker read higher; the PIC later confirmed the checker read more than 20 percent lower than the software. No per-battery comparison of the checker against a measured SoC was done for 2101 and 2088, so confidence is medium. Review change: outcome no_fault_found changed to determined. The reported mismatch was real and its cause (the checker's Li-ion SoC model applied to Amicell cells) is shown, as in VXEP-720; only the aircraft reading was not at fault.

event: 3rd SFG(A) VXE 557 gave off a strong burning smell from the fuselage three minutes after powering up on the ground (30 Oct 2024), with damage at the main battery power cable; no flight was involved.
component: AS150 anti-spark contact, fuselage power harness (107-102189) to main battery
failure_mode: Incomplete mate left the 6 ohm anti-spark contact carrying load current, so it overheated and melted
contributing: Possible out of spec AS150 sockets on the battery side (systemic AS150 issues VXEP-540 / VXEP-553)
Battery 3-1351 not returned for testing

evidence.quote: I do think that the OCT 30th incident is due to a bad mate between the fuse power harness and battery.
The anti-spark overheating/melting is a common symptom of a bad mate.
I was able to pull the logs from the oct 30th incident and noticed that the starting voltage is 13V with a 0.8A.
I don’t think we have enough information in the ppt to prove that the issue is isolated to the harness.
Three minutes into the aircraft being turned on a strong burning smell came from the inside of the aircraft.

team_root_cause:
- Poor Mating caused the incident OCT 30th 
- Melted anti-spark is a clear indication that a bad mate was made on the main battery. 
- When inserting the anti-spark pin into the socket the initial mate sees 6ohm to limit the inrush current and then once fully mated the connection should be around 2mohms. If the connection isn't completed quickly (i.e., the main contact isn't engaged in time), the small anti-spark contact may carry too much current for too long, causing it to overheat and melt.

would_settle_it.what: Melted anti-spark pin and contact condition on the fuselage power harness connector
Startup voltage and current trace showing the 13 V / 0.8 A start and the rise near 50 to 60 s
Measure AS150 socket dimensions and contact resistance on the battery side

attachments_read: 28221_AMENDED RMA Repair Quote for VXE-557 Fuselage Goodwill 3SFG 250127-1 April 14,, 2025.pdf.md
reasoning: The fuselage power harness was found damaged with a melted anti-spark contact, and the 30 Oct log starts at 13 V and 0.8 A, which the battery engineer said matches a bad initial mate. The anti-spark path is meant to carry current only briefly before the main contact engages, so a slow or incomplete mate overheats it. The harness was replaced, but the battery was never returned, so a socket defect on the battery side cannot be ruled out.
notes: Ticket covers two events. The 12 Oct 2024 flight (battery 3-1353, SoC fluctuating 16 to 30 percent on RTB) was split to VXEP-1136 and attributed there to an inaccurate SoC model valid only near 400 W / 30 A; it is not the main event here. Initiating cause set to operator_action (incomplete mate) with possible connector socket defect as contributing; the evidence does not separate the two. All RMA-478 scan PDFs have no text.

event: On two full-endurance fuel cell flights of VXE 732 (13 and 14 Nov 2024) the fuel cell stopped producing power from fuel starvation while the software still showed fuel remaining; one glide landing and one normal VTOL landing.
component: D450 fuel cell internal mass flow meter (fuel plumbed in reverse direction, reverse calibration)
failure_mode: Directionally sensitive mass flow meter plumbed backwards under-reported fuel consumed by about 10.8 to 13.3 percent, so the tank ran dry while fuel was shown remaining
contributing: Loss of fuel cell power did not trigger the fuel cell shutdown alert or automatic low-energy RTB
Early production defect affecting about 80 fielded units

evidence.quote: Upon performance of the test, both systems exhibited errors greater than 10% in the measurement
System’s D4500509 & D4500510 delivered initially August 2023, are among known 80 units
affected by manufacturing defect from early production that affected the plumbing of the fuel
The error % from this test is approximately 2.7%, which is within acceptable accuracy tolerance and
Post flight it was determined that the cause of the fuel cell error was fuel starvation.

team_root_cause: The primary root cause determined to be a manufacturing defect in the fuel routing through a directionally sensitive mass flow meter.  While plumbed in the correct flow orientation, the mass flow meter is able to accurately report fuel consumed within a 5% error margin.  When fuel is plumbed in the incorrect (reverse) direction, the measured fuel flow rate can become inaccurate, resulting in the under-reporting of fuel consumed.  The degree of inaccuracy is a function of the ambient temperature and fuel temperature at the time of use but is generally 8% to 13% over the -20°C to 50°C operationa
reasoning: Bench fuel sweeps against a calibrated mass flow sensor showed both returned fuel cells under-measuring fuel by more than 10 percent, matching the in-flight shortfall, and teardown found the fuel plumbed in reverse through the direction-sensitive flow meter from an early production defect. After re-plumbing and recalibration the error dropped to 2.7 percent on a full-tank endurance test. That is direct measurement plus a fix that removed the error.
notes: The report header reads Incident Number VIT2-500 / VXEP-732, which appears to be a typo for VXEP-780. The report says the reverse calibration is the suspected mechanism and the full scope is still under a QA CAR. Serial to flight mapping conflicts: the report pairs the 13 Nov AAR with D4500509, while the operator in ENG-2984 says 13 Nov flew S/N 510 and 14 Nov S/N 509. D4500509 stack also failed during return testing and was re-stacked (separate finding). The ENG-2984 report copy is identical to the VXEP-780 copy.

event: Molson VXE 637 flew with altitude panels disagreeing by about 500 ft and would not descend in orbit as expected; the operator landed by VTOL without damage.
component: GCS DTED elevation data (missing from GCS laptop)
failure_mode: With no DTED the launch calibration used 0 ft MSL instead of 515 ft as the reference elevation, offsetting altitudes by about 500 ft and making GCS MSL displays disagree
contributing: GCS shows inconsistent MSL altitudes when flown without DTED (GCSS-383, not fixed)
My GCS DTED folder contents apparently deleted and repopulated during GCS uninstall/reinstall, cause not proven

evidence.quote: The elevation for the launch area in this flight should have been 515ft MSL but due to missing DTED 0ft MSL was used instead.
There was not any DTED data loaded on the GCS laptop.
The laptop we used clearly had files missing in it.
This points to the My GCS folder, or at least its contents, being deleted, and then repopulated by a GCS install.
The GCS shows incorrect MSL altitudes in various places when the vehicle is launched without DTED.

reasoning: Logs showed the launch reference elevation was 0 ft MSL instead of the 515 ft terrain height, matching the 500 ft discrepancy, and the engineer reproduced the display error in HIL without DTED. The operator confirmed the DTED folder on that laptop was nearly empty. How the DTED files went missing was never proven.
notes: Initiating cause unknown: engineers suspected an uninstall/reinstall of GCS versions removed the DTED files, or user error, but could not reproduce it with the 6.3.4 installer.

event: LM test flights of VXE 732 with MCM (VCSi/OGCS 1.0) climbed far above the commanded landing pattern altitudes (over 900 ft AGL in IP4) when landing patterns were entered; operator intervened and the aircraft landed normally.
component: VSM 1.0 landing pattern preview / altitude encoding (MCM)
failure_mode: Landing patterns previewed before vehicle reference altitude was set were encoded without subtracting the about 2,500 ft reference elevation, so commanded altitudes jumped to about 2,863 to 2,873 ft
contributing: Fix (MS-395) existed in VSM 1.1 but aircraft flew the 1.0 release
Third, smaller climb near landing attributed to a thermal

evidence.quote: The AltitudeSet jumps from 410 to 2863 at 12:00:26.
the landing patterns were previewed prior to the vehicle having been calibrated.
Garret’s notes indicated that there were strong thermals encountered during their tests; I suspect that this uncommanded climb was the result of encountering one of these shortly before landing.
The first two were inadvertently commanded due to a software defect and the last one is suspected as being environmental in nature.
Prevent Previews of landing patterns if reference altitude has not been set.

team_root_cause: The LM pilots found a vulnerability in the 1.0 release of the VSM in which Landing Patterns could be Previewed prior to vehicle reference elevation being established by the OGCS.  As a result, the waypoints in the landing patterns were encoded approximately 2,500 feet higher than expected (the same amount as the reference elevation in MSL).  This defect was addressed in https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/MS-395 on September 4 and is now part of the 1.1 release.  @David Grosher
reasoning: VSM logs show landing patterns previewed at 10:06 and 10:07, before the reference altitude of 2502 ft MSL was set at 10:09, and the commanded altitude jumped to about 2,863 ft each time a pattern was first entered. That equals terrain height plus 300 ft without the reference subtracted, which is the known 1.0 defect fixed by MS-395. The third climb happened in RTB with throttle near idle and was attributed to a thermal.
notes: Ticket covers three excursions on 19 Nov 2024: two commanded by the software defect (main event) and one uncommanded climb near landing attributed to thermals. Ticket was canceled after root cause was communicated to LMCO.
